name: Niki Parmar
milestone_by_age_26: Joined Google in 2015 at age 24 as a software engineer on Google Brain—the youngest member of her team and the only one without a PhD—and by 2017 (age ~26) was an equal co-author of the seminal NeurIPS paper 'Attention Is All You Need' that introduced the Transformer architecture.
early_history_summary: Born in Pune, India, Parmar taught herself programming after missing admission to the Indian Institutes of Technology. She earned a master's in computer science from the University of Southern California and joined Google in 2015, quickly contributing to deep learning systems for search and ads before co-authoring the Transformer paper with Google colleagues.
family_context_summary: Grew up in a lower-middle-class family in a modest home in Pune, India; sources emphasize self-teaching and limited institutional pedigree rather than family wealth.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources as domain-expert parents; early path described as self-taught coding from home.
primary_early_advantage_tags: self-taught coder, Google Brain at 24, Transformer co-author, USC MS, Pune origins
evidence_summary: Multiple secondary profiles state Parmar joined Google at 24 in 2015 as the youngest and only non-PhD member of her team, implying birth around 1991. Within two years she was an equal co-author on 'Attention Is All You Need,' among the most cited papers in AI history. Early constraint (missed IIT, self-study in Pune) plus embedding in Google Brain's frontier research team and collaboration with peers (Vaswani, Shazeer, Uszkoreit, and others) formed the early-advantage stack. Later co-founded Adept AI and Essential AI and has worked at Anthropic.
starting_point: Born in Pune, India, into a lower-middle-class household; taught herself coding after missing IIT admission.
current_position: AI researcher/entrepreneur; Member of Technical Staff at Anthropic after co-founding Essential AI and Adept AI; co-author of the Transformer architecture paper.

trajectory.event: Joined Google as a software engineer and became the youngest member of her Google Brain team without a PhD.
Equal co-author of 'Attention Is All You Need,' introducing the Transformer architecture that underpins modern LLMs.
Co-founded Adept AI with former Google colleagues to build AI agents for software tools.
Co-founded Essential AI focused on enterprise AI systems.
Received the NEC C&C Prize with Transformer co-authors for pioneering generative-AI foundational research.
Joined Anthropic as Member of Technical Staff.

name: Russell A. Brown
milestone_by_age_26: Invented the N-localizer for CT-guided stereotactic neurosurgery in May 1978 as a third-year University of Utah medical student—a material technical invention—but birth year is not documented in reviewed sources, so age ≤26 cannot be independently verified with two sources.
early_history_summary: As a third-year medical student at the University of Utah in 1978, Brown invented the N-localizer under mentor James A. Nelson and built a prototype CT-compatible stereotactic frame. The concept became the Brown-Roberts-Wells (BRW) system widely used in neurosurgery and radiosurgery.
evidence_summary: The 1978 N-localizer invention is well documented (Wikipedia, Cureus, University of Utah radiology history) and was achieved as a medical student, which typically implies age mid-20s. Because no birth year appears in reviewed sources, age at the milestone cannot be confirmed as ≤26 under the two-source rule; marked ineligible pending birth-year verification.

name: Dario Amodei
milestone_by_age_26: No material career milestone by age 26 found. Amodei (born 1983) made the USA Physics Olympiad team in 2000 (age ~17) and received a Hertz Fellowship in 2007 (age ~24), but his PhD was completed in 2011 (age ~28), industry roles at Baidu/Google began around 2014–2015 (age ~31–32), OpenAI leadership later, and Anthropic was co-founded in 2021 (age ~38).
early_history_summary: Born in San Francisco to an Italian-American craftsman father and Jewish-American project-manager mother; graduated Lowell High School; attended Caltech then Stanford (BS physics); earned a biophysics PhD at Princeton (2011) as a Hertz Fellow; postdoc at Stanford Medicine before industry AI roles.
family_context_summary: Father Riccardo Amodei was an Italian-American leather craftsman from Tuscany who died when Dario was a young adult; mother Elena Engel is a Jewish American who worked as a library project manager. Not a high-capital tech dynasty.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were not AI/tech-domain experts; academic excellence appears self-driven within a middle-class professional household.
evidence_summary: Early academic excellence (Physics Olympiad team, Hertz Fellowship, Princeton PhD) is real but the rubric requires a material, independently verifiable career milestone by 26. Amodei's defining industry and founding milestones (Baidu, Google Brain, OpenAI VP of research, Anthropic CEO) all occurred after age 26.

name: Gabe Newell
milestone_by_age_26: Dropped out of Harvard and joined Microsoft in 1983 at age 20–21 (about the 271st employee), then produced the first major releases of the Windows operating system (Windows 1.0 in 1985 at age 22–23; Windows 2.0 in 1987 at age 24–25), a material early contribution to mainstream PC software.
early_history_summary: Born in Aspen, Colorado, and raised in Davis, California; began programming in high school while planning a medical path. Enrolled at Harvard in 1980, visited a brother at Microsoft, and at Steve Ballmer's urging left school in 1983 to join Microsoft as a programmer/producer on early Windows.
family_context_summary: Son of Donald Newell; grew up in Davis, California; worked paperboy and Western Union messenger jobs. Family financial status not richly documented beyond ordinary middle-class markers.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented as a software dynasty; brother worked at Microsoft and facilitated the introduction that led to Newell's hire.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Harvard, early Microsoft employee, Windows producer, Ballmer introduction, PC software wave
evidence_summary: Newell entered Microsoft at ~21 after a Harvard dropout path facilitated by family proximity to Microsoft and Ballmer. Producing early Windows placed him inside the dominant PC software wave with scarce systems experience. After 13 years and Microsoft wealth, he co-founded Valve in 1996 (age 33) with Mike Harrington, shipped Half-Life (1998), and later built Steam into the dominant PC digital distribution platform.
starting_point: Born in Aspen, Colorado (1962) and raised in Davis, California; son of Donald Newell; ordinary teen jobs (paperboy, Western Union) before Harvard.
current_position: Co-founder and president of Valve; major Steam shareholder; estimated net worth ~$11B (Forbes 2025); owns marine research firm Inkfish, Starfish Neuroscience, and yacht builder Oceanco.

trajectory.event: Dropped out of Harvard and joined Microsoft as an early employee, beginning work that led to producing early Windows releases.
Contributed as producer on Windows 1.0, helping establish Windows as a platform.
Left Microsoft with Mike Harrington to co-found Valve and self-fund Half-Life development.
Valve released Half-Life, a critical and commercial breakthrough FPS.
Launched Steam digital distribution, which later dominated PC game downloads.
Received BAFTA Fellowship and AIAS Hall of Fame recognition for industry impact.
Forbes estimated ~$11B net worth with majority Valve ownership; continued marine and neuroscience ventures.

name: Kimbal Musk
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded Zip2 (initially Global Link Information Network) with brother Elon Musk and Greg Kouri in 1995 at age 22–23, building online city-guide software for newspapers; the company sold to Compaq for about $307 million in 1999 when Kimbal was 26–27.
early_history_summary: Born in Pretoria, South Africa, to engineer/property developer Errol Musk and model/dietitian Maye Musk. After Pretoria Boys High School he joined Elon in Canada, studied business at Queen's University (graduated 1995), ran a College Pro Painters franchise, then co-founded Zip2 in Silicon Valley the same year.
family_context_summary: Son of Errol Musk (South African electromechanical engineer, pilot, property developer, emerald dealer) and Maye Musk (model and dietitian). Family had substantial local resources at times but also instability; father provided early Zip2 seed capital.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father's engineering and entrepreneurial background and seed capital supported early tech ventures; mother was a high-profile model/dietitian rather than a tech operator.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Elon Musk cofounder, Zip2, South Africa to Canada/SV, early web wave, family seed capital
evidence_summary: Kimbal's breakout was co-founding Zip2 at 22–23 with Elon during the early consumer internet wave in Palo Alto. Family seed money and a high-trust sibling cofounder, plus Queen's business training and painting-business cash, enabled the venture. After the Compaq exit he invested early in X.com/PayPal, later built restaurants (The Kitchen), food-education nonprofit Big Green, and urban farming company Square Roots, and sits on Tesla and SpaceX boards.
starting_point: Born in Pretoria, South Africa (1972) to engineer/entrepreneur Errol Musk and model/dietitian Maye Musk; raised with siblings Elon and Tosca.
current_position: Restaurateur and food-systems entrepreneur (The Kitchen Restaurant Group, Big Green chair, Square Roots); Tesla and SpaceX board member; major Tesla shareholder.

trajectory.event: Graduated Queen's University and co-founded Zip2 with Elon Musk and Greg Kouri in Palo Alto.
Zip2 sold to Compaq for about $307 million, providing early liquidity.
Opened The Kitchen community bistro in Boulder, Colorado, shifting into restaurants and food systems.
Co-founded Big Green (originally The Kitchen Community) to build school Learning Gardens nationwide.
Joined Chipotle Mexican Grill board (served until 2019) and continued Tesla/SpaceX board roles.
Co-founded Square Roots urban farming company using hydroponic shipping-container farms.

name: Jay Alammar
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Alammar is best known for the June 2018 blog post 'The Illustrated Transformer' and later work as Director and Engineering Fellow at Cohere (LLM University, Hands-On Large Language Models co-author); birth year is undocumented and the breakthrough educational work appears mid-career after software engineering experience.
early_history_summary: Software engineer by training who began serious machine-learning study after TensorFlow's open-sourcing (2015). Built a widely used visual blog explaining neural architectures, then joined Cohere to lead education and research communication around LLMs.
evidence_summary: The Illustrated Transformer (2018) is a major educational milestone but, without a birth year, cannot be aged to ≤26; his self-description as a software engineer who entered ML after 2015 implies a later-career pivot rather than a teen prodigy path.
